definition: The largest Security+ domain, covering the day-to-day work of keeping an organization secure: hardening and baselining systems, managing assets, finding and fixing vulnerabilities, monitoring and alerting, tuning enterprise security tools, identity and access management, automation, incident response, and investigation data sources.
example: A security analyst who applies a hardened baseline to new laptops, reviews SIEM alerts, patches a critical CVE, and then documents an incident is doing Domain 4.0 work.
keyPoints: Worth 28% of the exam, the biggest single domain; objectives 4.1 to 4.9; many questions are "given a scenario" (4.1, 4.5, 4.6, 4.9), so expect to pick the right tool or action; ties together prevention (hardening), detection (monitoring) and response

term: SY0-701 4.1: Given a scenario, apply common security techniques to computing resources
definition: This objective covers how to secure individual computing resources: building and keeping secure baselines, hardening different device types, securing wireless and mobile devices, choosing wireless security settings, writing secure applications, sandboxing, and monitoring.
example: A company rolling out tablets to field staff enrolls them in MDM under a COPE model, applies a hardened baseline, uses WPA3-Enterprise on office Wi-Fi and requires a VPN on public networks.
keyPoints: Scenario objective: pick the right technique for the device or situation; know the baseline life cycle (establish, deploy, maintain); know BYOD vs COPE vs CYOD; know WPA3, RADIUS and EAP basics

definition: A secure baseline is a documented, approved set of security settings (services, permissions, patches, policies) that a system type must meet. It gives every system of that type the same known-good starting point and a reference to measure drift against.
example: A company defines a Windows 11 workstation baseline that disables SMBv1, enforces BitLocker and sets password policy, then checks every laptop against it.
keyPoints: Life cycle: establish, deploy, maintain; often built from CIS Benchmarks or vendor guides; drift from the baseline is a finding to fix; a baseline is per system type, not one for everything

definition: Establishing a baseline means deciding and documenting the secure configuration for a system type, usually starting from trusted guidance such as CIS Benchmarks or manufacturer security guides and adjusting it to business needs.
example: The security team starts from the CIS Benchmark for Ubuntu Server, removes settings that would break the web app, and records the approved list as the server baseline.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Secure baselines
keyPoints: First step of the baseline life cycle; based on industry or vendor guidance plus testing; must be documented and approved; output is the reference for deploy and maintain

definition: Deploying a baseline means applying the approved settings to systems consistently, usually with central tools such as Group Policy, MDM, configuration management or golden images rather than by hand.
example: An administrator pushes the workstation baseline to 2,000 domain computers with Active Directory Group Policy objects.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Secure baselines
keyPoints: Use automation for consistency at scale (Group Policy, MDM, Ansible, images); manual setup invites drift and mistakes; deployment happens after the baseline is established and tested

definition: Maintaining a baseline means keeping it current and keeping systems compliant with it: updating it for new patches, threats and software versions, and regularly checking systems for configuration drift.
example: After a new OS release changes default settings, the team revises the baseline and runs a compliance scan that flags 40 servers which no longer match.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Secure baselines
keyPoints: Baselines are not set and forget; update when software, threats or guidance change; scan for drift (SCAP and compliance tools help); changes to the baseline go through change management

definition: The kinds of systems that must be hardened, meaning their attack surface is reduced by removing unneeded services and software, changing defaults, patching and restricting access. They range from user devices (workstations, mobile devices) and network gear (routers, switches) to servers and cloud infrastructure, and to specialised systems that are hard to patch (ICS/SCADA, embedded systems, RTOS, IoT devices).
example: Before deployment, a team disables unused ports on switches, removes default accounts from routers, and turns off unneeded services on servers.
keyPoints: Common steps for all: patch, change default credentials, disable unused services and ports, least privilege, logging; each target has its own constraints (ICS cannot be patched easily, IoT may not be patchable at all); hardening reduces attack surface

definition: Hardening phones and tablets means keeping the OS and apps updated, requiring screen locks and encryption, limiting app sources, and managing settings centrally through MDM so lost or stolen devices can be locked or wiped.
example: An MDM policy forces a 6-digit passcode, full device encryption, automatic updates and remote wipe on all company phones.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
keyPoints: MDM is the main tool to enforce mobile hardening; segment work and personal data (containerization); updates depend on carrier and manufacturer support; remote wipe for loss or theft

definition: Hardening desktops and laptops means applying regular OS and application patches, removing unnecessary software, enforcing least privilege (no daily admin rights), and running endpoint protection such as antivirus or EDR, plus host firewall and disk encryption.
example: IT removes local admin rights from users, enables BitLocker, turns on the host firewall and installs EDR on every laptop.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
keyPoints: Patch management and automatic updates; remove unneeded apps and services; standard user accounts, not admin; endpoint protection, host firewall and encryption, usually enforced with Group Policy

definition: Hardening a network switch means changing default credentials, using secure management (SSH instead of Telnet, SNMPv3), disabling unused ports, keeping firmware updated, and using port security or 802.1X to control what connects.
example: An administrator shuts down every unused switch port, enables 802.1X on user ports and disables Telnet in favor of SSH for management.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
keyPoints: Default passwords and plaintext management (Telnet, HTTP, SNMPv1/v2c) are classic exam findings; disable unused ports; firmware updates; restrict management access to a management network

definition: Hardening a router means changing default credentials, using encrypted management, disabling unused services and interfaces, applying firmware updates, and using access control lists to filter traffic and limit who can manage the device.
example: A network engineer applies an ACL so only the IT management subnet can SSH to the edge router and updates its firmware to fix a known flaw.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
keyPoints: Like switches: defaults, encrypted management, firmware; ACLs filter traffic and management access; routers sit at network boundaries, so a compromise affects many hosts

definition: Hardening cloud infrastructure means securing the customer-controlled parts of the cloud: least-privilege identity and access policies, secure configuration of storage and network security groups, MFA on admin accounts, logging, and endpoint protection on cloud instances.
example: A security review finds a storage bucket open to the public and an admin account without MFA; both are fixed and cloud audit logging is enabled.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
keyPoints: Shared responsibility: the customer still secures its configuration, identities and data; misconfiguration (public buckets, open security groups) is the top cloud risk; least privilege on IAM roles; enable logging and monitoring

definition: Hardening servers means patching the OS and applications, removing unneeded services and software, enforcing strong authentication and least privilege for administrators, using host firewalls and endpoint protection, and monitoring logs.
example: A new web server is built with only the web service installed, remote desktop restricted to a jump host, and the host firewall allowing only ports 443 and management traffic.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
keyPoints: Minimize installed roles and services; strict admin access and MFA; patching cadence plus monitoring; servers hold valuable data, so they are prime targets

definition: Industrial control systems (ICS) and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems run physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing. Because they often run old software that cannot be patched or rebooted easily, they are hardened mostly by network segmentation and strict access control.
example: A water utility places its SCADA network on an isolated segment with no direct internet access and only one tightly controlled jump server.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
keyPoints: Segmentation or air gaps are the main control; availability and safety come first, so patching is slow and must be planned; legacy protocols often lack authentication; compromise can cause physical harm

definition: Embedded systems are computers built into a device for one purpose, such as a printer, medical device or car controller. They often have limited updates and resources, so hardening relies on firmware updates from the manufacturer where available, changing defaults, and isolating them on the network.
example: A hospital puts its infusion pumps on a separate network segment because the manufacturer releases firmware updates only rarely.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
keyPoints: Limited or no patching, so segment them; change default credentials; depend on the vendor for firmware; often overlooked in inventories

definition: A real-time operating system (RTOS) is an operating system built to respond to inputs within strict, predictable time limits, used in things like industrial controllers, vehicles and medical equipment. It is hardened by isolating it on the network, applying vendor updates carefully, and limiting access, since added security software could affect timing.
example: A factory robot controller runs an RTOS; it is placed on an isolated network and updates are tested before installation so timing is not disrupted.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
keyPoints: RTOS = deterministic timing; often embedded, so hard to patch; isolate it and limit access; security tools must not break timing guarantees

definition: Internet of Things (IoT) devices are network-connected everyday devices such as cameras, smart sensors, thermostats and speakers. They often ship with weak defaults and poor update support, so they are hardened by changing default credentials, updating firmware, disabling unused features and placing them on a separate network segment.
example: Smart cameras in an office are moved to their own VLAN with no access to the corporate network, and their default admin passwords are changed.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Hardening targets
keyPoints: Default credentials are a classic IoT weakness (Mirai botnet); segment IoT onto its own network; update firmware where possible; buy from vendors with security support

definition: Securing wireless devices starts with how access points are installed: planning placement, coverage and channels so the network performs well and does not leak signal where attackers can use it.
example: Before installing access points in a new office, the network team does a site survey and reviews a heat map to place APs where coverage is good but signal does not spill into the parking lot.
keyPoints: Installation considerations include site surveys and heat maps; goal is good coverage, minimal interference and minimal signal leakage; also find rogue APs during surveys

definition: Installation considerations are the planning steps before and after placing wireless access points, mainly site surveys and heat maps, to decide AP location, channels and power levels and to spot interference and unauthorized APs.
example: A warehouse full of metal racks needs a site survey to see where signal is blocked before choosing AP locations.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless devices
keyPoints: Two listed tools: site surveys and heat maps; check for interference from other networks and devices; adjust channels and power; repeat surveys as the building or usage changes

definition: A wireless site survey examines a location to learn how radio signals behave there: existing networks, interference, obstacles and channel use. It guides where to place access points and can also reveal rogue or unknown access points.
example: A technician walks a building with a wireless analyzer, finds a neighboring network on the same channel and an unauthorized AP plugged in by an employee.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless devices > Installation considerations
keyPoints: Done before installation and periodically after; identifies interference, channel overlap and rogue APs; often produces the data used for heat maps

definition: A wireless heat map is a visual floor plan that shows signal strength in colors, making it easy to see strong coverage, dead zones and places where signal leaks outside the intended area.
example: A heat map shows strong red coverage reaching the street outside, so the team lowers AP power on that side of the building.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless devices > Installation considerations
keyPoints: Visual output of a site survey; shows coverage gaps and signal leakage; used to adjust AP placement and power; do not confuse with a SIEM dashboard

definition: Mobile solutions are the ways an organization secures smartphones and tablets: managing them with MDM, choosing a deployment (ownership) model such as BYOD, COPE or CYOD, and securing how they connect (cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth).
example: A company picks a COPE model, enrolls every phone in MDM, and requires a VPN when phones use public Wi-Fi.
keyPoints: Three parts: MDM, deployment models, connection methods; ownership model decides how much control the company has; MDM enforces policy whatever the model

definition: MDM is a centralized system for managing and securing mobile devices: enrolling them, pushing security policies (passcodes, encryption), controlling apps, separating work and personal data, tracking location, and remotely locking or wiping lost devices.
example: An employee loses a company tablet in a taxi; IT uses the MDM console to locate it and then remotely wipe it.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions
keyPoints: Enforces policy centrally on many devices; features: remote wipe, geolocation, app allow lists, containerization (work data separated from personal); works with BYOD, COPE and CYOD

definition: Mobile deployment models define who owns a device and how it may be used. Security+ lists bring your own device (BYOD), corporate-owned personally enabled (COPE) and choose your own device (CYOD).
example: A company weighs BYOD to save money against COPE for more control over the data on each phone.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions
keyPoints: BYOD: user owns it; COPE: company owns and supplies it, personal use allowed; CYOD: user picks from an approved list, company owns it; more company ownership means more control and less user privacy concern

definition: BYOD is a model where employees use their own personal devices for work. It saves the company hardware costs but makes control harder, so work data is usually separated with MDM containerization and the user must accept company policies.
example: Staff use their own iPhones for work email, with the company app container that IT can wipe without touching personal photos.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Deployment models
keyPoints: User owns the device; hardest to control and secure, with many device types to support; privacy conflict when the company wants to wipe or monitor; containerization separates work data

definition: COPE is a model where the company buys, owns and manages the device but allows the employee to use it for personal activities too. The company keeps full control and can wipe it, since the device is company property.
example: A firm hands every salesperson a company-owned phone that is fully managed but may also be used for personal apps and calls.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Deployment models
keyPoints: Company owns and chooses the device; personal use allowed; company has full control; vs CYOD: in COPE the company picks the device, in CYOD the user picks from an approved list

definition: CYOD is a model where the employee chooses a device from a company-approved list, and the company buys, owns and manages it. It balances user choice with company control and support.
example: New hires can pick either an approved Android or iPhone model; the company purchases it and enrolls it in MDM.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Deployment models
keyPoints: User chooses, but only from an approved list; company owns and manages it; middle ground between BYOD and COPE; trap: CYOD does not mean the user owns it

definition: Connection methods are the ways mobile devices communicate, each with its own risks. Security+ lists cellular, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
example: A phone may be on the carrier network, then join hotel Wi-Fi, while paired to a Bluetooth headset, creating three separate attack paths.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions
keyPoints: Cellular: carrier network, traffic bypasses corporate monitoring; Wi-Fi: rogue APs, evil twins, on-path attacks, use encryption or VPN; Bluetooth: short range, pairing attacks, disable when not needed

definition: Cellular connections use a mobile carrier network (such as 4G or 5G). Traffic between the phone and the tower is usually encrypted (in 4G the carrier can choose to turn this off), but it bypasses the company network, so corporate filtering and monitoring cannot see it, and devices can be tracked by location.
example: An employee tethers a laptop to a phone hotspot, sending traffic over cellular and around the corporate web filter.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Connection methods
keyPoints: Bypasses corporate security controls; location tracking risk; SIM swapping and fake cell towers are related threats; control with MDM and VPN policies

definition: Wi-Fi connects mobile devices to local wireless networks. Public or unknown networks risk eavesdropping, rogue access points, evil twins and on-path attacks, so devices should use strong wireless encryption and a VPN on untrusted networks.
example: A user joins "Free_Airport_WiFi", which is actually an attacker's evil twin AP capturing their traffic.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Connection methods
keyPoints: Prefer WPA3 or at least WPA2 encrypted networks; VPN on public Wi-Fi; watch for evil twin and rogue APs; MDM can restrict which networks devices join

definition: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless link used for headsets, watches and file transfer. Risks include unwanted pairing, bluejacking (sending unsolicited messages) and bluesnarfing (stealing data), so it should be turned off or set non-discoverable when not needed and pairing should be controlled.
example: An attacker in a cafe uses a flaw in an unpatched phone's Bluetooth stack to read its contacts.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Mobile solutions > Connection methods
keyPoints: Short range, but still an attack path; bluejacking = unsolicited messages, bluesnarfing = data theft; disable or make non-discoverable; keep devices patched

definition: Wireless security settings decide how a Wi-Fi network authenticates users and protects traffic. Security+ covers WPA3, AAA with RADIUS, cryptographic protocols and authentication protocols.
example: A company configures WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X, authenticating users against a RADIUS server tied to Active Directory.
keyPoints: Personal mode uses a shared passphrase, enterprise mode uses 802.1X with RADIUS and individual credentials; WPA3 replaces WPA2; know which protocol does encryption vs authentication

definition: WPA3 is the current Wi-Fi security standard. In personal mode it replaces the WPA2 pre-shared key exchange with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE), which resists offline password guessing and gives forward secrecy; it also requires protected management frames and offers a stronger 192-bit enterprise mode.
example: An attacker captures a WPA3-Personal handshake but cannot run an offline dictionary attack on it, unlike with a WPA2-PSK handshake.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless security settings
keyPoints: SAE (dragonfly handshake) replaces the PSK 4-way handshake guessing weakness; forward secrecy: a later stolen password does not decrypt old captures; WPA3-Personal still requires at least AES-CCMP-128, like WPA2; the optional WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode uses AES-GCMP-256; study guides teach "WPA3 uses GCMP", so pick GCMP if asked; WPA3 is the best answer for new Wi-Fi; on Wi-Fi 7 gear WPA3 moves to GCMP-256 with the SAE-EXT-KEY key management even in personal mode, so "WPA3 uses GCMP" is fully true there; in the 6 GHz band (Wi-Fi 6E and 7) WPA3 and protected management frames are mandatory and WPA2 is not allowed; transition mode lets WPA2 and WPA3 clients share one network name, but the WPA2 clients keep WPA2 protection

definition: AAA stands for authentication, authorization and accounting. RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is a common AAA protocol: the access point passes the user's login to a central RADIUS server, which checks credentials (often against Active Directory) and logs the session.
example: With WPA3-Enterprise, each employee logs in to Wi-Fi with their own domain account, verified by the RADIUS server, so a departing employee is blocked by disabling one account.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless security settings
keyPoints: Used in enterprise Wi-Fi with 802.1X; RADIUS uses UDP (1812 authentication, 1813 accounting); it hides only the password, while TACACS+ (TCP 49) encrypts the whole message body (RFC 8907 calls this obfuscation and advises running it over a secure transport); early RADIUS used UDP 1645 and 1646; individual credentials beat a shared passphrase

definition: Wireless cryptographic protocols encrypt and integrity-protect Wi-Fi traffic. WPA2 uses CCMP, based on AES; WPA3-Personal requires at least AES-CCMP-128, and the WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode uses the stronger AES-GCMP-256. Old options such as WEP and TKIP are broken and should not be used.
example: An audit finds an old access point still offering TKIP; it is reconfigured to allow only AES-based encryption.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless security settings
keyPoints: CCMP-128 (AES) for WPA2 and the WPA3-Personal minimum, GCMP-256 for WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit (study guides shorten this to "WPA3 uses GCMP"); WEP and TKIP are insecure; cryptographic protocol = protects data, authentication protocol = proves identity; Wi-Fi 7 uses GCMP-256 for WPA3-Personal and WPA3-Enterprise, keeping CCMP-128 only for backward compatibility

definition: Wireless authentication protocols prove who is connecting. Enterprise Wi-Fi uses IEEE 802.1X port-based access control with the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) family, such as EAP-TLS (certificates on both sides), PEAP and EAP-TTLS (a TLS tunnel protecting another login method) and EAP-FAST.
example: A company uses EAP-TLS so each laptop presents its own certificate to the RADIUS server before joining Wi-Fi.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Wireless security settings
keyPoints: 802.1X is the framework, EAP carries the method, RADIUS checks the credentials; EAP-TLS needs client and server certificates and is the strongest; PEAP and EAP-TTLS need only a server certificate; EAP-FAST (designed by Cisco) builds its tunnel from a shared secret called a Protected Access Credential (PAC) instead of requiring certificates

definition: Application security means building software so it resists attack. Security+ 4.1 lists input validation, secure cookies, static code analysis and code signing as techniques.
example: A development team validates all form input, sets secure cookie flags, runs a static analyzer in its build pipeline and signs its release installer.
keyPoints: Four techniques: input validation, secure cookies, static code analysis, code signing; these are developer-side protections; 4.3 covers application security as a way to find vulnerabilities

definition: Input validation checks every piece of data an application receives (type, length, format, allowed characters) and rejects or cleans anything unexpected before using it. It is a key defense against injection attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, working together with parameterized queries and output encoding, which OWASP names as the main fixes for those two.
example: A login form rejects a username containing ' OR 1=1 -- because only letters and digits are allowed, stopping a SQL injection attempt.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Application security
keyPoints: Validate on the server side (client-side checks are easy to bypass); prefer allow lists over deny lists; defends against SQL injection, XSS, buffer overflows; pair with parameterized queries (SQL injection) and output encoding (XSS); on the exam, input validation is the usual answer for stopping injection

definition: A secure cookie is a browser cookie protected with attributes: Secure (sent only over HTTPS), HttpOnly (not readable by page scripts, which limits theft through XSS) and SameSite (limits sending it with cross-site requests). They protect session tokens and other sensitive values stored in cookies.
example: A web app marks its session cookie Secure and HttpOnly, so it is never sent over plain HTTP and an XSS script cannot read it.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Application security
keyPoints: Secure flag = HTTPS only; HttpOnly = no JavaScript access; SameSite helps against cross-site request forgery; do not store sensitive data in cookies in plain text; SameSite values: Strict (sent only on requests from the same site), Lax (also sent when the user follows a link from another site; Chromium-based browsers use it when no value is set), None (always sent, and the cookie must also be Secure)

definition: Static code analysis, also called static application security testing (SAST), examines source code without running it to find security flaws such as injection risks, buffer overflows and hard-coded secrets, often automatically in the build pipeline.
example: A static analyzer flags a line where user input is concatenated into a SQL query before the code is ever deployed.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Application security
keyPoints: Code is not executed (vs dynamic analysis, which runs the app); finds issues early in development; produces false positives that need human review; cannot find runtime or configuration problems

definition: Code signing is when a developer digitally signs software with a private key tied to a certificate from a trusted certificate authority. Users and systems verify the signature with the public key to confirm who published the code and that it has not been changed since it was signed.
example: Windows shows the verified publisher name when installing a signed application, and warns if a downloaded installer was altered after signing.
category: 4.1 Security techniques for computing resources > Application security
keyPoints: Provides integrity and authenticity (who signed it, unchanged since); does not prove the code is safe or bug-free; relies on protecting the private signing key; uses public key infrastructure

definition: Sandboxing runs an application or file in an isolated, restricted environment so it cannot reach the rest of the system or network. It limits damage from untrusted code and is used for testing, malware analysis and in browsers and mobile apps.
example: A suspicious email attachment is opened inside a sandbox, where analysts watch it try to contact a command-and-control server without risking the real network.
keyPoints: Isolation contains damage; used by browsers, mobile OSs, and malware analysis; test new code in a sandbox before production; virtual machines and containers are common ways to sandbox

definition: Monitoring computing resources means continuously collecting and reviewing logs, performance data and security events from systems so problems and attacks are detected quickly. Secure baselines and hardening reduce risk, and monitoring confirms they keep working.
example: An admin sees in the logs that a hardened server suddenly has a new service listening and investigates.
keyPoints: Detective control that complements preventive hardening; logs feed a SIEM; watch for configuration drift and unusual activity; 4.4 goes deeper into monitoring tools

term: SY0-701 4.2: Explain the security implications of proper hardware, software, and data asset management
definition: This objective covers managing assets through their whole life: buying them securely, assigning owners and classifications, tracking and inventorying them, and disposing of them so no data is left behind.
example: An organization buys laptops only from approved vendors, tags each one to an owner, tracks it in an inventory, and gets a certificate of destruction when its drive is shredded.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management
keyPoints: Asset life cycle: acquisition, assignment, tracking, disposal; you cannot protect what you do not know you have; know sanitization vs destruction vs certification

definition: Acquisition or procurement is how an organization buys hardware, software and services. A secure process uses approved vendors, checks security requirements and supply chain risk before purchase, and records new assets so they enter management from day one.
example: A purchase request for new network switches must go through IT and security approval, use a vetted vendor, and the switches are added to inventory on arrival.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management
keyPoints: Security should be part of purchasing, not added later; approved vendor lists reduce supply chain risk; prevents shadow IT; new assets go straight into inventory

definition: Assignment and accounting mean recording each asset against a responsible owner and a classification, so the organization knows who is accountable for it and how it must be protected.
example: Each laptop record lists the employee responsible and the department that owns it, and each database is labeled with its data classification.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management
keyPoints: Two parts: ownership and classification; supports accountability; classification drives which controls apply

definition: Ownership means a specific person or group is named as responsible for an asset, including its security, approving access and deciding how it is used.
example: The HR director is listed as owner of the payroll system and must approve every access request to it.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Assignment/accounting
keyPoints: Every asset needs a named owner; the owner is accountable, even if IT runs the system day to day; unowned assets tend to go unpatched and unmonitored

definition: Classification labels an asset or its data by sensitivity and importance (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted) so the right protection is applied.
example: A server holding customer credit card data is classified as restricted, so it requires encryption, extra monitoring and limited access.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Assignment/accounting
keyPoints: Classification decides controls, handling and disposal method; set by the owner; data classifications are covered more in 3.3

definition: Asset tracking keeps an up-to-date view of every asset the organization has, where it is, who has it and its status, using inventory records and automated discovery (enumeration).
example: An asset management system shows 1,050 laptops issued, while a network scan finds 1,080, revealing 30 unrecorded devices.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management
keyPoints: Two parts: inventory and enumeration; finds lost, stolen and unauthorized devices; accurate tracking is the base for patching and vulnerability scanning

definition: An inventory is the recorded list of assets with details such as asset tag, serial number, owner, location, configuration and software installed, kept current as assets change.
example: Each laptop has an asset tag and a record listing its serial number, assigned user and OS version in the inventory database.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Monitoring/asset tracking
keyPoints: The record of what you have; must be updated when assets move or change; supports audits, patching and incident response

definition: Enumeration is actively discovering and listing assets, for example by scanning the network or querying management tools, to find what is really present, including devices and software missing from the inventory.
example: A discovery scan enumerates all devices on the network and finds an unknown wireless access point an employee plugged in.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Monitoring/asset tracking
keyPoints: Discovers what is actually there, compared with the inventory, which records what should be there; finds shadow IT and rogue devices; done with scanners and agents

definition: Disposal or decommissioning is retiring an asset securely: removing it from service and inventory and making sure no data on it can be recovered, through sanitization or destruction, with proof (certification), while keeping any data the organization must retain.
example: Old servers are retired: required records are archived, drives are wiped or shredded, a certificate of destruction is filed, and the inventory is updated.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management
keyPoints: Four parts: sanitization, destruction, certification, data retention; data left on discarded drives is a common breach; NIST SP 800-88 guides media sanitization

definition: Sanitization makes data on storage media unrecoverable for a chosen level of effort, while the media can usually be reused. NIST SP 800-88 (Rev. 2 of September 2025, which replaced the 2014 Rev. 1 and keeps the same three methods) names them: clear (overwrite or factory reset; stops simple recovery and normally keeps the media usable), purge (the drive's own sanitize commands such as block erase or cryptographic erase, or degaussing for magnetic media; defeats even laboratory recovery and may keep the media usable) and destroy (the media can no longer store data).
example: Before donating old laptops, IT runs a secure erase on each SSD so the drives can be reused without exposing data.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Disposal/decommissioning
keyPoints: Sanitization can keep the device usable, destruction cannot; simple file deletion or quick formatting is not sanitization; overwriting an SSD is weak because of spare cells, so use its built-in sanitize or cryptographic erase; degaussing works only on magnetic media, can ruin hard drives and does nothing to SSDs; Rev. 2 points to the IEEE 2883 standard for the right technique per media type; for cloud or other virtual storage, cryptographic erase may be the only purge option

definition: Destruction physically ruins storage media so data cannot be recovered even in a laboratory and the media can never store data again, for example by disintegrating, incinerating, melting, pulverizing or shredding. It suits the most sensitive data and media that has failed or cannot be sanitized.
example: Failed hard drives from a bank's card processing servers are sent to a vendor that disintegrates them into small particles.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Disposal/decommissioning
keyPoints: Physical, permanent, media not reusable; vs sanitization, which removes data but can keep the media usable; drilling a hole or bending a drive only partly damages it, so NIST does not count it as destroy; often done by a third party who then provides certification; NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 warns that shredding and pulverizing lose effectiveness as media gets denser and should be used only for the lowest-sensitivity data, and that degaussing is not an approved destroy technique

definition: Certification is documented proof that media was properly sanitized or destroyed, often a certificate of destruction from a disposal vendor listing the assets, method and date.
example: A recycling vendor provides a certificate of destruction listing the serial numbers of 200 shredded drives, which the company keeps for its auditors.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Disposal/decommissioning
keyPoints: Provides evidence for audits and compliance; NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 (September 2025, section 4.6) calls it a certificate of sanitization, completed for each sanitized device and kept on paper or electronically, and lists what it records (manufacturer, model and serial number, media type, method and technique, tool and version, verification method, who did it and when); especially important when a third party does the disposal; ties disposal back to inventory records

definition: Data retention means keeping data for the period required by law, regulation or business policy, and disposing of it once that period ends. Before an asset is destroyed, any data that must be kept is preserved elsewhere.
example: Before wiping an old finance server, seven years of financial records required by regulation are moved to an archive.
category: 4.2 Hardware, software, and data asset management > Disposal/decommissioning
keyPoints: Keep data as long as required, but not longer (extra data is extra risk); legal holds can override normal disposal; retention policy should be checked before sanitization or destruction

term: SY0-701 4.3: Explain various activities associated with vulnerability management
definition: This objective covers the vulnerability management cycle: finding vulnerabilities, analyzing and prioritizing them, responding and remediating, validating that fixes worked, and reporting.
example: A team scans weekly, confirms findings, ranks them by CVSS and business impact, patches or applies compensating controls, rescans to verify, and reports progress to management.
keyPoints: Cycle: identify, analyze, respond, validate, report; know false positive vs false negative; CVE is the identifier, CVSS is the score; remediation options include patching, segmentation, compensating controls, insurance, exceptions

definition: Identification methods are the ways an organization discovers vulnerabilities: vulnerability scans, application security testing, threat feeds, penetration testing, responsible disclosure programs and system or process audits.
example: A company combines automated scans, a yearly penetration test, a bug bounty program and threat intelligence feeds to find weaknesses.
keyPoints: No single method finds everything; scans are automated and broad, pen tests are manual and deep; threat feeds tell you about new threats; audits check processes as well as systems

definition: A vulnerability scan uses an automated tool to check systems for known weaknesses such as missing patches, misconfigurations and open services, comparing what it finds against a database of known vulnerabilities. Scans can be credentialed or non-credentialed, and internal or external.
example: A weekly scan reports that 12 servers are missing a critical OpenSSL patch.
keyPoints: Credentialed scans log in and see more (fewer false positives); non-credentialed shows the attacker view; scans identify, they do not exploit (that is pen testing); keep scanner signatures updated

definition: In vulnerability management, application security means finding flaws in software, through static analysis of code, dynamic analysis of the running application, and package monitoring of third-party components.
example: A company runs SAST on each code commit, DAST against its staging site, and monitors its open-source libraries for new CVEs.
keyPoints: Three methods: static analysis, dynamic analysis, package monitoring; static = code not running, dynamic = running app; package monitoring covers dependencies and the software supply chain

definition: Static analysis (SAST) inspects source code or binaries without running them to find vulnerabilities such as injection flaws, unsafe functions and hard-coded credentials.
example: A static analysis tool reports that a function uses strcpy without bounds checking, a possible buffer overflow.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Application security
keyPoints: No execution; finds flaws early and points to the exact line; can produce false positives; misses runtime and environment problems that dynamic analysis catches

definition: Dynamic analysis (DAST) tests an application while it is running, sending inputs and observing behavior to find vulnerabilities such as injection, authentication flaws and crashes. Fuzzing, which sends large amounts of random or malformed input, is a common form.
example: A fuzzer sends thousands of malformed requests to a web API and finds one that crashes the service.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Application security
keyPoints: App is running (vs static: code only); finds runtime and configuration issues; fuzzing is a dynamic technique; does not point to the exact line of code

definition: Package monitoring tracks the third-party libraries and packages an application uses and alerts when one has a known vulnerability or is compromised, so it can be updated or replaced.
example: A dependency monitoring tool alerts the team that a logging library in their app has a newly published critical CVE.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Application security
keyPoints: Covers software supply chain risk from open-source and third-party code; often uses a software bill of materials (SBOM) or software composition analysis; verify packages come from trusted sources

definition: A threat feed is a stream of threat intelligence, such as new vulnerabilities, malicious IP addresses, domains and file hashes, and attacker techniques, that helps an organization learn about threats relevant to it. Feeds come from open sources, commercial vendors, sharing organizations and the dark web.
example: A SIEM imports a threat feed of known malicious IPs and alerts when a workstation connects to one.
keyPoints: Sources: OSINT, proprietary/third-party, information-sharing organizations, dark web; often shared in standard formats such as STIX over TAXII; feeds are only useful if relevant and acted upon

definition: OSINT is intelligence gathered from publicly available sources such as websites, social media, news, public vulnerability databases, forums and government advisories. It is free but must be checked for accuracy.
example: An analyst follows public vulnerability advisories and security researchers' blogs to learn about a new exploit the same day it is published.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Threat feed
keyPoints: Public and free (vs proprietary, paid); quality varies, so verify it; attackers use OSINT too, for reconnaissance

definition: A proprietary or third-party threat feed is commercial threat intelligence from a security vendor, usually paid, often curated, more timely and tailored, and delivered in formats ready to load into security tools.
example: A company subscribes to a vendor feed that pushes newly seen malicious domains straight into its firewall and SIEM.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Threat feed
keyPoints: Paid and curated (vs OSINT, free and public); may include vendor research not available elsewhere; still needs tuning to be relevant

definition: An information-sharing organization is a group where members, often in the same industry or sector, share threat intelligence with each other, such as an Information Sharing and Analysis Center (ISAC) or government programs.
example: A bank receives a warning from the financial sector ISAC about a phishing campaign that hit another member bank yesterday.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Threat feed
keyPoints: Industry focused, so very relevant; members share what they see; examples: sector ISACs, government partnerships such as CISA programs

definition: The dark web is the part of the internet reachable only through special software such as Tor. Monitoring it can reveal stolen credentials, leaked company data, or attackers planning or selling access to an organization.
example: A dark web monitoring service finds employee usernames and passwords from the company for sale on a criminal forum, so passwords are reset.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Threat feed
keyPoints: Early warning of breaches and leaked credentials; often done by specialized services; content is hard to verify and access carries risks

definition: A penetration test is an authorized, simulated attack where testers actively try to exploit vulnerabilities to show what a real attacker could achieve. It follows agreed rules of engagement and may be done with known, partially known or unknown knowledge of the environment.
example: Hired testers exploit an unpatched web server, move to a database, and report how they reached customer data.
keyPoints: Exploits vulnerabilities (a scan only identifies them); needs written authorization and rules of engagement; known (white box), partially known (gray box), unknown (black box) environment; more in 5.5

definition: A responsible disclosure program gives outside researchers a clear, safe way to report vulnerabilities they find to the organization, which then has time to fix them before details are made public.
example: A researcher finds a flaw in a company's website and reports it through the published security contact page instead of posting it online.
keyPoints: Defines how to report and what is allowed; gives the vendor time to patch before public disclosure; bug bounty programs add rewards; reduces chance of a flaw being made public before it is fixed

definition: A bug bounty program pays rewards to outside researchers who find and responsibly report vulnerabilities in an organization's systems, within a defined scope and rules.
example: A software company pays a researcher $5,000 for reporting an authentication bypass in its mobile app.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Identification methods > Responsible disclosure program
keyPoints: Rewarded form of responsible disclosure; scope and rules define what may be tested; adds many testers at low cost; out-of-scope testing is not authorized

definition: A system or process audit reviews systems, configurations and procedures against policies, standards or regulations to find gaps, such as missing controls, weak processes or noncompliant settings.
example: An internal audit finds that the account removal process takes weeks, so former employees keep access, a process vulnerability.
keyPoints: Finds process weaknesses that scanners cannot; compares against a standard or policy; can be internal or external

definition: Analysis is deciding what each discovered vulnerability really means: confirming it is real, scoring and classifying it, and prioritizing it based on severity, exposure, the environment, business impact and the organization's risk tolerance.
example: Two findings share a CVSS 9.8, but one is on an internet-facing server and the other on an isolated lab system, so the internet-facing one is fixed first.
keyPoints: Steps: confirm, classify, score, prioritize; CVSS alone is not enough, context matters; inputs include exposure factor, environmental variables, organizational impact, risk tolerance

definition: Confirmation checks whether a reported vulnerability actually exists before effort is spent fixing it, weeding out false positives and considering whether real issues were missed (false negatives).
example: An analyst checks the server version by hand and finds the scanner wrongly flagged a patched service.
keyPoints: Verify before acting; false positive = reported but not real; false negative = real but not reported; credentialed scans and manual checks improve accuracy

definition: A false positive is when a scanner or security tool reports a vulnerability or threat that does not actually exist. It wastes time but does not leave the organization exposed.
example: A scanner reports a vulnerable Apache version because it reads the banner, but the server has a backported security patch.
keyPoints: Reported but not real; wastes effort, causes alert fatigue; reduce with credentialed scans, updated signatures and tuning; less dangerous than a false negative

definition: A false negative is when a real vulnerability or threat exists but the scanner or security tool does not detect it. It is more dangerous because the organization believes it is safe.
example: A scan reports a server as clean, but it is vulnerable to a flaw the scanner's outdated signatures do not cover.
keyPoints: Real but missed; most dangerous error because nothing gets fixed; caused by outdated signatures, non-credentialed scans, limited scope; combine methods (scans plus pen tests)

definition: Prioritizing means ordering vulnerabilities for remediation, since not everything can be fixed at once, based on severity scores, whether exploits exist, how exposed the system is and how important the affected asset is.
example: A team fixes an actively exploited flaw on its public VPN gateway before a higher-scored flaw on an isolated internal test machine.
keyPoints: Fix highest risk first, not simply highest score; consider active exploitation, exposure and asset value; limited time and staff make prioritization necessary

definition: CVSS is a standard way to rate the severity of a vulnerability with a score from 0.0 to 10.0, built from metrics such as attack vector, complexity, privileges needed, user interaction and impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability. It is maintained by FIRST.
example: A vulnerability that is remotely exploitable without credentials and gives full system control gets a CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.8, rated Critical.
keyPoints: Score, not an identifier (CVE is the identifier); v3.x and v4.0 (published November 2023) use the same ratings: None 0.0, Low 0.1 to 3.9, Medium 4.0 to 6.9, High 7.0 to 8.9, Critical 9.0 to 10.0; base score can be adjusted with environmental metrics (v4.0 metric groups: Base, Threat, Environmental, Supplemental); NVD publishes CVSS scores for CVEs

definition: CVE is a public list that gives each publicly known vulnerability a unique identifier, such as CVE-2021-44228, so everyone refers to the same flaw by the same name. The program is run by MITRE and sponsored by CISA, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
example: A vendor advisory, a scanner report and a news article all reference CVE-2021-44228, so the team knows they all mean the Log4Shell flaw.
keyPoints: Identifier, not a score (CVSS is the score); format CVE-year-number; officially named Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, but CompTIA's acronym list writes Enumeration; scanners map findings to CVE IDs

definition: Vulnerability classification groups vulnerabilities by type or category, such as injection, misconfiguration, missing patch, or weak cryptography, and by severity, so similar issues can be handled together and root causes found.
example: Classification shows that 60% of findings are misconfigurations, pointing to a weak baseline process rather than missing patches.
keyPoints: Classifies by type (for example using CWE categories) and severity; helps find root causes and patterns; supports reporting and prioritization

definition: Exposure factor (EF) is the percentage of an asset's value that would be lost if a specific threat succeeded, expressed from 0% to 100%. It is used in quantitative risk calculations: single loss expectancy (SLE) equals asset value times exposure factor.
example: If a $100,000 database would lose 40% of its value in a breach, the EF is 0.4 and the SLE is $40,000.
keyPoints: EF is a percentage of value lost; SLE = AV x EF; ALE = SLE x ARO; higher exposure means higher priority

definition: Environmental variables are facts about where a vulnerable system sits and how it is used, such as whether it is internet-facing, what data it holds, and which other controls protect it, that make the real risk higher or lower than the generic score. CVSS has environmental metrics for this.
example: A critical flaw on a server that is offline, isolated and behind multiple controls is lower real risk than the same flaw on a public web server.
keyPoints: Adjusts generic severity to your environment; the same CVE can be urgent in one company and minor in another; CVSS environmental metrics capture it

definition: Industry or organizational impact is how much a vulnerability being exploited would hurt this particular organization, considering its industry, regulations, critical services, reputation and the data involved.
example: A flaw in a patient records system has higher impact for a hospital, due to health data regulations and patient safety, than the same flaw would have elsewhere.
keyPoints: Business context drives priority; regulated industries (health, finance) face fines and legal impact; critical services and safety raise impact

definition: In vulnerability management, risk tolerance decides how long a vulnerability of each severity may stay open and when an unfixed one may be accepted. It turns the organization's overall tolerance into remediation deadlines and exception rules.
example: A low-risk-tolerance bank requires critical vulnerabilities to be patched within 48 hours, while a startup allows 30 days.
keyPoints: Set by leadership; shapes remediation timelines and whether exceptions are allowed; same idea as risk tolerance in 5.2 (the acceptable variation from risk appetite), applied here to deciding which findings must be fixed first and how fast

definition: Response and remediation is deciding and carrying out what to do about each vulnerability: fix it by patching, reduce it with segmentation or compensating controls, transfer financial risk with insurance, or formally accept it with an exception or exemption.
example: A legacy system that cannot be patched is placed on an isolated segment with extra monitoring, and a documented exception is approved.
keyPoints: Options: patching, insurance, segmentation, compensating controls, exceptions and exemptions; patching is preferred when possible; every option except patching leaves the flaw in place

definition: Patching applies vendor updates that fix the vulnerability itself. It is the most direct remediation, but patches should be tested and deployed through change management, with a rollback plan.
example: After Microsoft releases a fix for a critical flaw, IT tests it on a pilot group and then deploys it to all servers.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Vulnerability response and remediation
keyPoints: Fixes the root cause; test before broad deployment; automate where possible; some systems (legacy, ICS, embedded) cannot be patched, so other controls are needed

definition: Cybersecurity insurance transfers some of the financial impact of a security incident to an insurer. It does not fix the vulnerability, but it helps cover costs such as recovery, legal fees and some losses.
example: A company buys cyber insurance that helps pay for incident response and customer notification after a ransomware attack.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Vulnerability response and remediation
keyPoints: Risk transfer, not risk reduction; does not remove the vulnerability; insurers often require baseline controls such as MFA and backups; policies may exclude some events

definition: Segmentation places a vulnerable system on a separate, restricted network segment so attackers have fewer paths to reach it and a compromise cannot spread easily. It is often used when a system cannot be patched.
example: An old manufacturing PC running an unsupported OS is moved to its own VLAN that can reach only the machine it controls.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Vulnerability response and remediation
keyPoints: Limits exposure without fixing the flaw; common for legacy, ICS and IoT systems; implemented with VLANs, firewalls, ACLs

definition: A compensating control is an alternative safeguard used when the normal fix is not possible, reducing the risk to an acceptable level by other means.
example: Since a vulnerable application cannot be patched until next quarter, a web application firewall rule is added to block the known exploit.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Vulnerability response and remediation
keyPoints: Used when the primary control (often patching) is not possible; examples: WAF rules, extra monitoring, segmentation, disabling a feature; should be documented and reviewed

definition: An exception or exemption is a formal, documented approval to leave a vulnerability unremediated, or not follow a policy, for a stated reason and usually for a limited time, with the risk accepted by someone with authority.
example: A critical medical device cannot be updated without vendor approval, so management signs a six-month exception while compensating controls are applied.
category: 4.3 Vulnerability management > Vulnerability response and remediation
keyPoints: Formal risk acceptance; must be documented, approved, time limited and reviewed; often paired with compensating controls; an undocumented unpatched system is not an exception; NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4 asks that exceptions be tracked closely and suggests putting unpatchable assets in their own maintenance group with other mitigations rather than leaving them as open-ended exceptions

definition: Validation of remediation confirms that a fix actually worked and did not create new problems, by rescanning, auditing and verifying the system's state.
example: After patching, the team rescans the servers, confirms the finding is gone, and closes the ticket.
keyPoints: Three methods: rescanning, audit, verification; never assume a patch worked; validation closes the loop before reporting

definition: Rescanning means running the vulnerability scan again after remediation to confirm the vulnerability no longer appears and no new issues were introduced.
example: A rescan after patching shows the critical finding has disappeared from all but one server, where the patch failed.
keyPoints: Fastest way to confirm a fix; use the same scan settings as the original scan; can reveal failed patches or new findings

definition: An audit, as validation, reviews records, configurations and remediation evidence to confirm fixes were done correctly and according to policy and compliance requirements.
example: An auditor checks change tickets and system configurations to confirm every critical vulnerability was fixed within the policy deadline.
keyPoints: Checks that the process was followed and documented, not only that a scan is clean; supports compliance; can be internal or external

definition: Verification confirms by direct checking that a remediation is in place and effective, for example by checking the installed version, testing that the exploit no longer works, or confirming a compensating control is active.
example: A tester tries the original exploit against the patched server and confirms it now fails.
keyPoints: Direct confirmation the fix is effective; can include manual testing or retesting by the pen tester; complements rescans

definition: Vulnerability reporting communicates findings, risk levels, remediation progress and trends to the right audiences, from technical detail for administrators to summary metrics for management and compliance.
example: A monthly report shows management that critical vulnerabilities dropped from 45 to 8 and average time to patch fell to 6 days.
keyPoints: Tailor to the audience (technical vs executive); track metrics such as open criticals and time to remediate; supports compliance and accountability; final step of the cycle

term: SY0-701 4.4: Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools
definition: This objective covers what to monitor (systems, applications, infrastructure), the monitoring activities (log aggregation, alerting, scanning, reporting, archiving, alert response) and the tools used (SCAP, benchmarks, agents, SIEM, antivirus, DLP, SNMP traps, NetFlow, vulnerability scanners).
example: A SOC collects logs from servers, apps and firewalls into a SIEM, tunes its alerts, quarantines an infected laptop, and archives logs for a year.
keyPoints: Know what each tool does and its look-alikes (SIEM vs NetFlow vs SNMP; agent vs agentless); alert tuning reduces false positives; quarantine is a response action

definition: Monitoring computing resources means watching the health, performance and security events of systems, applications and infrastructure so that problems and attacks are noticed and handled quickly.
example: A monitoring dashboard shows a server's CPU at 100%, a spike of failed application logins and a router interface going down, all at the same time.
keyPoints: Three areas: systems, applications, infrastructure; covers both availability and security; feeds log aggregation and alerting

definition: Monitoring systems means watching servers and endpoints: their availability, resource use (CPU, memory, disk), security logs, logins, running processes and configuration changes.
example: Monitoring alerts when a domain controller logs hundreds of failed logins from one account in a minute.
category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Monitoring computing resources
keyPoints: Watch OS logs, authentication events, resource use and changes; sudden changes can indicate compromise or failure

definition: Monitoring applications means watching application availability, response times, errors and application logs, including security events such as failed logins, access to sensitive functions and unusual transactions.
example: Application logs show a single user downloading thousands of customer records, triggering an alert.
category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Monitoring computing resources
keyPoints: App logs show what users do inside the app; watch errors and unusual usage; uptime and performance matter for availability too

definition: Monitoring infrastructure means watching the network devices and supporting systems, such as routers, switches, firewalls, wireless controllers, and cloud and virtualization platforms, for availability, performance and security events.
example: An alert fires when a core switch reports an interface error spike and the firewall shows a flood of blocked connections.
category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Monitoring computing resources
keyPoints: Covers network and platform components; uses SNMP, NetFlow, device logs; infrastructure failure affects many systems at once

definition: The alerting and monitoring activities are log aggregation, alerting, scanning, reporting, archiving, and alert response and remediation or validation (including quarantine and alert tuning).
example: A SOC collects logs, alerts on suspicious events, runs scans, reports metrics, archives old logs, and responds to alerts by quarantining hosts.
keyPoints: Think of a pipeline: collect, alert, respond, report, keep; each activity has a separate card; SIEM supports most of them

definition: Log aggregation collects logs from many sources, such as servers, applications, firewalls and endpoints, into one central place, usually a SIEM or log server, where they can be searched, correlated and kept safe from tampering.
example: Firewall, VPN and Active Directory logs are all sent to a SIEM, so an analyst can see a VPN login followed by unusual file access in one view.
keyPoints: Centralizes logs for correlation and search; protects logs from being erased on a compromised host; often uses syslog; accurate time sync (NTP) is needed to correlate events

definition: Alerting automatically notifies staff when monitored data matches a rule or threshold that suggests a problem or attack, so it can be investigated quickly.
example: The SIEM sends an alert when an administrator account logs in at 3 a.m. from another country.
keyPoints: Rules and thresholds trigger alerts; too many alerts cause alert fatigue; tuning keeps alerts useful; alerts lead to response

definition: Scanning as a monitoring activity regularly checks systems and networks for vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, unauthorized devices and compliance with baselines.
example: A nightly scan finds a server whose configuration no longer matches its secure baseline.
keyPoints: Regular and automated; finds vulnerabilities, rogue devices and drift; results feed alerts and reports

definition: Reporting summarizes monitoring data into useful information, such as security events, trends, compliance status and incidents handled, for analysts, managers and auditors.
example: A weekly SIEM report shows the top attacked systems and the number of blocked malware events.
keyPoints: Turns raw data into decisions; scheduled or on demand; supports compliance; dashboards show near-real-time views

definition: Archiving stores older logs and monitoring data long term, protected from change, to meet legal and compliance retention requirements and to support later investigations.
example: Logs older than 90 days move from the SIEM to cheaper archive storage and are kept for one year as required by policy.
keyPoints: Retention set by policy or regulation; archived data must stay intact and searchable when needed; helps investigate incidents discovered long after they began

definition: Alert response is what happens after an alert: investigating it, containing the problem (for example quarantine), fixing it, validating the fix, and improving the alerts themselves through tuning.
example: An alert on a malware detection leads an analyst to quarantine the laptop, clean it, confirm it is clean and adjust the rule that fired late.
keyPoints: Listed parts: quarantine and alert tuning; validate before closing; feedback from each alert improves detection

definition: Quarantine isolates a suspicious file, device or system so it cannot spread malware or reach other resources while it is investigated and fixed.
example: EDR automatically cuts an infected laptop off from the network, allowing only communication with the security console.
category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Activities > Alert response and remediation/validation
keyPoints: Containment action; can apply to files (antivirus moves them) or to whole hosts (network isolation); keeps evidence for investigation

definition: Alert tuning adjusts detection rules and thresholds to cut false positives while still catching real threats, so analysts are not overwhelmed and important alerts are not missed.
example: A rule alerting on every failed login is tuned to alert only after 10 failures in 5 minutes from one source.
category: 4.4 Security alerting and monitoring > Activities > Alert response and remediation/validation
keyPoints: Reduces false positives and alert fatigue; over-tuning can create false negatives; an ongoing process, not a one-time fix

definition: The alerting and monitoring tools listed are SCAP, benchmarks, agents or agentless collection, SIEM, antivirus, DLP, SNMP traps, NetFlow and vulnerability scanners.
example: A SOC uses a SIEM for correlation, NetFlow for traffic patterns, SNMP traps for device faults and scanners for vulnerabilities.
keyPoints: Correlation across logs = SIEM; traffic metadata = NetFlow, device fault alerts = SNMP traps; configuration checks = SCAP and benchmarks, known flaws = vulnerability scanners; malware = antivirus, sensitive data leaving = DLP

definition: SCAP is a NIST suite of open standards that lets security tools describe vulnerabilities and configuration checks in a common format, so different tools can automatically check systems for compliance and known flaws. It includes standards such as CVE, CVSS, CPE, CCE, XCCDF and OVAL.
example: A compliance tool loads a SCAP content file for a benchmark and automatically checks 500 servers against it.
keyPoints: Created by NIST; enables automated, tool-independent compliance and vulnerability checks; common language between scanners; pairs with benchmarks; current release SCAP 1.4 (2026), which prefers CVSS v4.0; XCCDF holds the checklists, OVAL describes how to test a system, CPE names platforms and CCE names configuration settings

definition: Benchmarks are published, recommended secure configuration settings for specific operating systems, applications and devices, such as CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs. Systems are compared against them to find weak settings.
example: A scan compares a Linux server with the CIS Benchmark and reports that SSH root login is still allowed.
keyPoints: Common sources: CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs, vendor guides; used to establish secure baselines; often checked automatically with SCAP

definition: Agent-based monitoring installs software on each system to collect data and enforce settings continuously; agentless monitoring collects data remotely, for example over the network or through management interfaces, with nothing installed on the system.
example: An EDR agent runs on every laptop, while network devices that cannot run agents are monitored agentlessly through SNMP and syslog.
keyPoints: Agent: more detail, works offline and off network, but must be installed and maintained; agentless: nothing to install, good for devices that cannot run agents, but less detail and needs network access; NAC can use persistent or dissolvable agents too

definition: A SIEM collects and aggregates logs and events from across the organization, correlates them to find suspicious patterns, raises alerts, provides dashboards and reports, and keeps data for investigations and compliance.
example: The SIEM correlates a phishing email click, a new process on the same laptop, and a connection to a known bad IP into one high-priority alert.
keyPoints: Key functions: aggregation, correlation, alerting, dashboards, retention; correlation across sources is what sets it apart; needs tuning; SOAR (4.7) automates response on top

definition: Antivirus software detects, blocks and removes malware on endpoints using signatures of known malware plus heuristic and behavior-based detection, and reports detections to central monitoring.
example: Antivirus quarantines a malicious attachment and the central console alerts the security team.
keyPoints: Signature-based detection misses new malware, so heuristics and behavior help; keep definitions updated; EDR goes further with recording and response; alerts feed the SIEM

definition: As a monitoring tool, DLP watches data in use, in motion and at rest for sensitive information, such as card numbers or confidential documents, and alerts on or blocks attempts to send or copy it where it should not go.
example: DLP alerts the security team when an employee tries to email a spreadsheet full of Social Security numbers to a personal address.
keyPoints: Monitors data in use, in motion, at rest; detects patterns and labels of sensitive data; can alert or block; 4.5 covers DLP as a capability to configure

definition: An SNMP trap is an unsolicited alert message that a network device's SNMP agent sends to the management station when a specific event occurs, such as an interface going down or a threshold being crossed, instead of waiting to be polled.
example: A switch sends an SNMP trap to the network management system the moment a link to a server goes down.
keyPoints: Trap = device pushes an alert (vs polling, where the manager asks); traps use UDP 162, polling UDP 161; use SNMPv3 for authentication and encryption, v1 and v2c send community strings in clear text

definition: NetFlow is a protocol, originally from Cisco, that collects metadata about network traffic flows, such as source and destination addresses, ports, protocol, times and byte counts, and sends it to a collector for analysis. It shows who talked to whom and how much, not packet contents.
example: NetFlow data shows a workstation sending 20 GB to an unknown external IP overnight, suggesting data exfiltration.
keyPoints: Flow metadata, not full packet capture; good for baselining traffic, spotting exfiltration and DDoS; uses probes and collectors; IPFIX is the related open standard

definition: Vulnerability scanners are tools that automatically probe systems and applications for known vulnerabilities, missing patches and misconfigurations, and report findings with severity ratings, often mapped to CVE and CVSS.
example: A scheduled scanner run finds a web server with an expired TLS certificate and an outdated, vulnerable PHP version.
keyPoints: Identifies, does not exploit; credentialed vs non-credentialed; keep plugins updated; results can contain false positives that need confirmation

term: SY0-701 4.5: Given a scenario, modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security
definition: This objective covers changing and tuning enterprise security tools to improve protection: firewalls, IDS/IPS, web filters, operating system security, secure protocols, DNS filtering, email security, file integrity monitoring, DLP, NAC, EDR/XDR and user behavior analytics.
example: After spoofed emails impersonate the CEO, the company publishes SPF and DKIM records and a DMARC reject policy, and adds a web filter rule blocking newly registered domains.
keyPoints: Scenario objective: choose the right control and setting; know firewall rule order and implicit deny; know SPF vs DKIM vs DMARC; know secure protocol and port pairs

definition: A firewall controls traffic between networks or hosts by allowing or blocking it according to rules based on addresses, ports, protocols and, for next-generation firewalls, applications and users. Enhancing security means tuning its rules, access lists, allowed ports and protocols, and network zones such as screened subnets.
example: An admin replaces an "allow any" rule with rules that permit only HTTPS to the web server and block everything else.
keyPoints: Rules read top to bottom, first match wins, implicit deny at the end; least privilege for traffic; NGFW adds application awareness; screened subnet isolates public-facing servers

definition: Firewall rules are the individual statements that say which traffic to allow or deny, defined by source, destination, port, protocol and action. They are processed in order, the first match is applied, and traffic matching no rule is denied by an implicit deny.
example: A broad "allow all from LAN" rule placed above a specific "deny LAN to finance server" rule means the deny never takes effect.
keyPoints: Order matters: specific rules above general ones; first match wins; implicit deny at the bottom; remove unused and overly broad rules; NIST SP 800-41 notes rule handling varies by product: on sequential first-match firewalls, rules that match the most traffic should sit as high as correct ordering allows, for speed; NIST recommends deny by default

definition: Access control lists (ACLs) are ordered lists of permit and deny entries applied to an interface or traffic direction on a firewall or router, filtering packets by criteria such as IP address, port and protocol.
example: A router ACL permits traffic from the management subnet to port 22 and denies SSH from everywhere else.
keyPoints: Same logic as rules: ordered, first match, implicit deny; often stateless on routers; applied inbound or outbound per interface

definition: Firewalls filter by port number and protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP) to allow only the services that are needed, for example TCP 443 for HTTPS, while blocking others such as Telnet on TCP 23.
example: The firewall allows TCP 443 to the web server, but blocks TCP 3389 so Remote Desktop is not exposed to the internet.
keyPoints: Allow only needed ports and protocols; know common ports (22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 3389 RDP); port alone does not prove which application is in use, NGFWs inspect the application

definition: A screened subnet, formerly called a DMZ, is a separate network zone between the internet and the internal network that holds public-facing servers. Firewalls control traffic so outsiders reach only those servers, and a compromised server cannot freely reach the internal network.
example: The company web and email gateways sit in a screened subnet, and the firewall blocks them from starting connections to the internal database network.
keyPoints: Same idea as the older term DMZ; holds public services (web, email relay, DNS); limits damage if a public server is compromised; uses one firewall with three interfaces or two firewalls

definition: An intrusion detection system (IDS) watches traffic or host activity and alerts on attacks; an intrusion prevention system (IPS) sits inline and can also block them. They detect using signatures and anomaly or behavior analysis, and show trends over time.
example: An inline IPS drops packets matching a known exploit signature, while an IDS on a mirror port only alerts.
keyPoints: IDS = detect and alert (passive, out of band); IPS = inline, can block; signature-based misses new attacks, anomaly-based catches them but has more false positives; network-based vs host-based

definition: IDS/IPS trends are patterns in detections over time, such as rising attack types, top sources or most targeted systems, usually shown on dashboards. They help spot campaigns and decide where to strengthen defenses or tune rules.
example: The IPS dashboard shows a steady rise in attempts against the VPN gateway over two weeks, so the team prioritizes patching it.
keyPoints: Look at patterns, not single alerts; helps prioritize and tune; changes from normal can signal a new campaign
